'''''Lepidium didymum''''',  the '''lesser swine-cress''',<ref name=BSBI07>{{BSBI 2007 |accessdate=2014-10-17 }}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Brassicaceae]].

==Description==
''Lepidium didymum'' is an [[Annual plant|annual]] or [[Biennial plant|biennial]] herb<ref name=BRCBSBI>{{cite web|title=Online Atlas of the British & Irish flora: ''Coronopus didymus'' (Lesser swine cress) |publisher=Biological Records Centre and Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=London, U.K. |url=http://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/index.php?q=node/1681 |accessdate=15 July 2016 }}</ref> with decumbent or ascending and glabrous green stems, up to {{convert|40|cm}} long, radiating from a central position. The leaves are pinnate and alternate and can reach a length of {{convert|5|cm|0|abbr=on}}. It blooms between July and September. The flowers are inconspicuous, with four very short white petals or none at all, and 2 (rarely 4),<ref name=CTW>{{cite book |last1=Clapham |first1=A.R. |last2=Tutin |first2=T.G. |last3=Warburg |first3=E.F. |date=1981 |title=Excursion Flora of the British Isles |edition=Third |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=0521232902 }}</ref>{{rp|54}} stamens. The fruits consist of two rounded valves, notched at the apex, with a very short style between them.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book|last=Stace|first=C. A.|authorlink = Stace, C. A.|year=2010|title=New Flora of the British Isles|edition=Third|publisher=Cambridge University Press|location = Cambridge, U.K.| isbn=9780521707725}}</ref>{{rp|405}}<ref name=Gaby>Gaby H. Schmelzer, Gabriella Harriet Schmelzer and Ameenah Gurib-Fakim (Editors) {{google books|7FJqgQ3_tnUC|Medicinal Plants, Volume 1|page=362}}</ref> They are wrinkled and contain orange or reddish brown seeds, that are 1–5 mm long.<ref name=Gaby/>

==Taxonomy==
It was first described and published by the Swedish botanist [[Carl Linnaeus]] in 'Mant. Pl.' (Mantissa Plantarum) on page 92 in 1767.<ref>{{cite web|title=Brassicaceae Lepidium didymum L.|url=http://www.ipni.org/ipni/idPlantNameSearch.do?id=286148-1|publisher=ipni.org|accessdate=6 December 2017}}</ref><ref name="TPL_kew-2337750"/>

The [[Botanical name#Binary name|specific epithet]] ''didymum'', refers to the Greek word δίδυμα for 'twin' or 'in pairs',<ref>{{cite web|title=Botanary: didymum|url=https://davesgarden.com/guides/botanary/go/1847/|publisher=davesgarden.com|accessdate=6 December 2017}}</ref> referring to the seed capsule.

==Distribution==
''Lepidium didymum'' is of uncertain origin,<ref name=BRCBSBI/> but is often cited as native to South America,<ref name=Stace/><ref name=CTW/> mainly [[Argentina]], [[Bolivia]], [[Brazil]], [[Chile]], [[Paraguay]], [[Peru]], [[Uruguay]] and [[Venezuela]].<ref name=Grin>{{cite web|title=Taxon: Lepidium didymum L.|url=https://npgsweb.ars-grin.gov/gringlobal/taxonomydetail.aspx?id=423806|publisher=npgsweb.ars-grin.gov|accessdate=6 December 2017}}</ref> It has been introduced elsewhere as a weed of cultivation. It has naturalised across the globe, from Africa, Europe, Asia, Australasia, North America and South America.<ref name=Grin/> In Britain, it had been recorded from the wild by 1778,<ref name=BRCBSBI/> chiefly in England and the south of Ireland,<ref name=BSBI>{{cite web |title=BSBI Distribution maps:''Lepidium didymum'' |url=http://bsbi.org/maps?taxonid=2cd4p9h.6y1367#style=N4IgLgpgtgDgNgQ0gOQK5QEYQE4gFwgCMIAvkA |publisher=Botanical Society of Britain and Ireland |location=London, U.K. |accessdate=15 July 2016 }}</ref> growing on cultivated and waste ground, in gardens and lawns, by paths and roadsides.

==Uses==
The leaves of this plant are [[edible]], and have a salty, cress or mustard flavour.<ref name=widlfood>{{cite web |title=Lesser Swine Cress, Coronopus didymus, Lepidium didymum |url=https://www.wildfooduk.com/edible-wild-plants/lesser-swine-cress/ |website=Wild Food UK |access-date=5 May 2021}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Swinecress, Wart Cress: Micro Mustards |url=http://www.eattheweeds.com/coronopus-didymussquamatus-smelly-pot-herbs-2/ |website=Eat The Weeds and other things, too |access-date=5 May 2021 |date=25 December 2017}}</ref>
